It is active throughout encyclopedic/biographical, news and arts-or-business writing, where it peaks on the ordinary carrier words of those sentences - above all the indefinite article ' a'/' an', ' has', ' in', ' into', ' from', ' the', ' of', ' to', ' with', ' as', and the '.'/'\n' that closes a sentence or section - and on light content words of that field (' law', ' art', ' music', ' poetry', ' novel', ' film', ' career', ' teacher', ' compliance', ' appeared'); the same words carry no activation when they sit in episodic action narrative ('she walked into the room'), in physical/technical or object description ('the chemical engineer calibrated the spectrometer'), in mathematics or in code, which sit at baseline (~0.00 mean, versus ~0.18-0.24 mean in biography documents).

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Barbara Hepworth arrived in St Ives in 1939 and stayed for the rest of her life. Born in Wakefield in 1903, the daughter of a civil engineer, she had studied at the Leeds School of Art and then at the Royal College of Art, where she met Henry Moore and began a friendship that would shape the course of modern British sculpture. Her early carvings in wood and stone, made with a directness that owed as much to the example of Brancusi as to the lessons of her teachers, attracted attention in the press and the admiration of a small circle of collectors.

The move to Cornwall changed her work. The light, the stone and the sea entered her practice, and the shapes she carved became more open and more responsive to landscape. She appeared in several group exhibitions in London during the war years, but it was the series of stringed figures, made in the late 1930s and 1940s, that established her reputation. Each of them was a meditation on tension and enclosure, and each was made with the patience of a craft that she had learned as a student.

Her career spanned five decades, and it included commissions for schools, hospitals and public squares. She wrote of her work as a kind of poetry of form, and she insisted that the sculptor's task was to release the figure that lay inside the stone. In 1950 she represented Britain at the Venice Biennale, and in the years that followed her sculpture travelled to museums in Europe and North America. Critics who had once treated her as a follower of Moore began to describe her as an original, and her studio in St Ives became a place of pilgrimage for young artists.

The present exhibition brings together more than sixty works from every period of her career. It includes a group of plasters that have not been shown since the 1970s, a selection of drawings made in the hospital at St Ives during the war, and a reconstruction of the studio as it looked in the year of her death. A catalogue with essays by three scholars accompanies the show, and it places her work in the context of the wider history of European modernism.

Visitors who come to the exhibition expecting a survey of abstract sculpture will find instead a record of a working life. The tools are displayed beside the finished pieces, the notebooks are open at pages of sketches, and the photographs show the artist at work in a studio that was also a home. It is a generous way to present a career, and it makes the argument that the distinction between the domestic and the sculptural, which so much writing about modernism has taken for granted, was never one that Hepworth accepted.
